# Power Analysis of the Research Protocol

*Generated by `research/analysis/research_power.py`. Seed 20260827, 200,000 simulations per cell.*

This file is generated. Do not edit by hand; re-run the script.

This analyses **our process**, not any strategy. It asks what the protocol in
`BACKTESTING_PROTOCOL.md` would do if a real edge existed, and what it would do
if none did. No market data is involved.

---

## 1. Does the search even select the real edge?

A search over N candidates containing one genuinely-edged strategy and N-1
worthless ones. The winner is whichever scores best on the 5-year development
sample. Probability the winner is the *real* one:

| Trials | needle Sharpe 0.4 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| 5 | 46.0% | 59.8% | 71.6% | 80.3% |
| 10 | 31.2% | 45.5% | 59.6% | 71.3% |
| 25 | 18.2% | 30.8% | 45.2% | 58.8% |
| 50 | 11.8% | 22.3% | 36.1% | 50.0% |
| 100 | 7.5% | 16.0% | 28.2% | 41.9% |
| 250 | 4.1% | 10.0% | 19.7% | 32.7% |
| 500 | 2.5% | 7.0% | 15.1% | 26.7% |
| 1,000 | 1.6% | 4.7% | 11.3% | 21.7% |
| 5,000 | 0.5% | 1.9% | 5.5% | 12.7% |

**A larger search is a worse search.** Every additional worthless candidate is
another lottery ticket for noise, and noise has a 5-year standard error of 0.45
while a real Sharpe-0.6 edge only has a mean of 0.6. Past a few hundred trials
the search is, in effect, selecting the luckiest null strategy almost every time.

## 2. End-to-end power and false deployment

`Power` = P(the real edge is selected **and** clears every gate).
`False deploy` = P(a worthless strategy clears every gate), searches with no edge present.

| Trials | Power @ S=0.4 | @ S=0.6 | @ S=0.8 | @ S=1.0 | False deploy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5.1% | 13.9% | 27.3% | 42.7% | 0.2% |
| 5 | 0.6% | 3.0% | 9.0% | 19.2% | 0.0% |
| 10 | 0.3% | 1.4% | 5.3% | 13.1% | 0.0% |
| 25 | 0.1% | 0.6% | 2.7% | 7.8% | 0.0% |
| 50 | 0.0% | 0.3% | 1.6% | 5.2% | 0.0% |
| 100 | 0.0% | 0.1% | 0.9% | 3.4% | 0.0% |
| 250 | 0.0% | 0.1% | 0.5% | 2.1% | 0.0% |
| 500 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.3% | 1.4% | 0.0% |
| 1,000 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.2% | 0.9% | 0.0% |
| 5,000 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.1% | 0.4% | 0.0% |

The false-deployment rate stays low because the Deflated Sharpe gate widens as
trials increase -- that gate is doing its job. But it defends by raising the bar
for *everything*, so it suppresses real edges at the same time. The protocol
does not distinguish 'lucky' from 'good'; it only distinguishes 'extreme' from
'not extreme'.

## 3. If the protocol says ship it, is it real?

Positive predictive value, for a prior probability `p` that a real edge exists
among the candidates at all. Given how many people have looked for tradeable
crypto trend edges, a prior above ~20% is generous.

| Trials | PPV @ p=5% | @ p=20% | @ p=50% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 76.8% | 94.0% | 98.4% |
| 5 | 74.9% | 92.5% | 97.1% |
| 10 | 72.3% | 91.4% | 96.6% |
| 25 | 65.8% | 88.6% | 95.1% |
| 50 | 59.3% | 85.7% | 94.0% |
| 100 | 57.5% | 84.1% | 92.6% |
| 250 | 40.9% | 74.5% | 89.2% |
| 500 | 46.7% | 77.5% | 89.3% |
| 1,000 | 40.3% | 71.3% | 84.2% |
| 5,000 | 29.1% | 58.9% | 74.1% † |

† fewer than 200 simulated deployments in 1,000,000 runs -- Monte Carlo noise
dominates these cells; read them as "small", not as the printed digits.

PPV stays high across the grid, but for a reason that is not comfort: the
protocol almost never ships **anything**. Conditional on shipping, we are
probably right. Unconditionally, we are probably empty-handed -- see section 2.

## 4. The affordable trial budget

Largest trial count retaining a given end-to-end power, by the size of the edge
we are hoping to find. `max power` is what a **single pre-specified** candidate
achieves -- the ceiling, before any search cost at all.

| True Sharpe | max power (N=1) | N for 20% power | for 10% | for 5% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | 5.1% | **none** | **none** | 1 |
| 0.6 | 13.8% | **none** | 1 | 3 |
| 0.8 | 27.4% | 1 | 3 | 8 |
| 1.0 | 42.6% | 3 | 12 | 50 |
| 1.3 | 61.9% | 30 | 150 | 1000 |

**This is the finding that should change how we work.** Two things follow:

1. Against the edge size we actually expect (Sharpe 0.4-0.7,
   `STRATEGY_HYPOTHESES.md` sec.5.4), the protocol as written is close to
   unable to approve anything, *even with no search at all*. It is not
   calibrated for the effect size we are hunting.
2. Trials are a shared, exhaustible budget. A single 6-parameter sweep
   (15,625 trials) does not merely waste power -- it removes essentially all
   of it, permanently, for every hypothesis that follows on the same data.

## 5. Which gate does the damage?

Marginal pass rate of each gate against a strategy with a **genuine** Sharpe of
0.6, ignoring the selection step. A gate that rejects most real edges is buying
its safety expensively. Deflation thresholds shown at 10 and 100 trials.

| Gate | Passes a real S=0.6 edge |
|---|---|
| Dev plausibility screen (SR > 0.3) | 73.2% |
| Deflated Sharpe @ 10 trials (dev SR > 1.44) | 4.2% |
| Deflated Sharpe @ 100 trials (dev SR > 1.87) | 0.4% |
| Validation Sharpe > 0.4 | 60.2% |
| Walk-forward >= 5/8 windows positive | 73.7% |
| Cross-asset >= 4/5 same sign | 72.5% |
| Pooled OOS Sharpe > 0.4 | 65.4% |
| **All gates combined (10-trial deflation)** | **1.5%** |

The Deflated Sharpe gate is the binding constraint, and it is the one whose
severity we control directly -- through the trial count we choose to spend.
Note it tightens from 1.44 to 1.87 purely by going from 10 trials to 100:
that gap is the price of a sweep, paid by every real edge we might have had.
